claims.text: Under ethanol oxidation conditions, catalytic performance of nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts is governed by reaction-induced surface segregation.
Ir, Rh, or other constituent elements preferentially migrate toward the catalyst surface during ethanol oxidation.
Preferentially segregated elements form sub-nanometer clusters at the catalyst surface.
Surface clusters alter the adsorption energy of ethanol.
Surface clusters alter the adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The freshly prepared nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalyst is a homogeneous solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
Potential cycling or temperature variation can drive surface diffusion in PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles.
The high-entropy elemental mixture creates a distorted lattice.
Operating electrochemical conditions produce differential atomic mobilities among the alloy constituents.
Differential atomic mobilities promote selective surface segregation of elements having favorable bonding parameters under reaction conditions.
Cluster-induced changes in local adsorption energies alter ethanol-oxidation kinetics.
Formation of segregated surface clusters may reduce catalyst poisoning.
Surface regions that develop elemental clustering will exhibit higher catalytic currents than the freshly prepared homogeneous catalyst.
Surface regions that develop elemental clustering will exhibit modified product selectivity relative to the homogeneous catalyst.
In-situ characterization under segregation-promoting conditions will reveal regional surface enrichment in elements such as Ir or Rh.
The proposed mechanism operates when potential and temperature permit moderate surface diffusion but do not cause irreversible phase separation or catalyst dissolution.
The proposed mechanism requires the catalyst to remain nanoscale without extensive sintering.
